findings.title: Fresh installations bypass the GitHub installer identity check
findings.body: When the installation webhook has not yet created an `Integration`, this branch immediately advances the pipeline without checking the GitHub user that installed the app. The OAuth step and app-install step are separate browser interactions, so a user can authorize OAuth as one GitHub account and then install the app as another account (or simply win the race against webhook delivery); the subsequent integration creation has no installer identity to compare. This leaves the exact fresh-install/race case unprotected despite the new validation requirement. The pipeline must defer completion until a trusted installer identity is available, or otherwise obtain and validate it before creating the integration.

findings.title: Installer validation crashes for integrations without sender metadata
findings.body: The code indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally. Existing GitHub integrations, and integrations created through the normal build path when no webhook sender has been attached, can have metadata without `sender` (the updated basic-flow test itself expects metadata with no sender). If such an active integration exists without an organization integration, for example during recovery/reinstallation or after an older installation, this produces a KeyError and returns a 500 instead of the intended failed-installation response. Treat missing sender information as an unverifiable installation and return `error` (or implement a safe migration/lookup).

findings.title: OAuth exchange and user lookup failures are not converted to installation failures
findings.body: Only parsing `safe_urlread` is protected by the try block. `safe_urlopen` can fail for GitHub HTTP/network errors, and `get_user_info` can fail when GitHub rejects the newly exchanged token or its `/user` request fails. Those exceptions escape the pipeline and result in a 500, rather than the failed-installation page promised for invalid/reused codes or token generation failures. Catch the relevant HTTP/API exceptions around both the exchange and user-info request and return `error`.
